daily.ideas: Market Strategy: Rate Reactions; Economic Viewpoint: US FOMC (15-16 September)

news.h: YTL Power secures four more Siemens gas turbines to meet rising regional energy and AI demand
news.body: YTL Power International Bhd said it has acquired four additional gas turbine units from Siemens Energy via reservation agreements. The new reservations add to the three units previously secured by YTL Power, bringing the total to seven units, with a combined capacity of over 5,250MW, to support power generation projects in Malaysia and the wider region. The deal supports YTL Power's efforts to meet growing regional energy needs, driven by industrial growth, electrification, and the rapid expansion of data centres and AI. It also strengthens YTL Power's existing investments in digital infrastructure, including data centres, YTL AI Cloud and AI models developed by YTL AI Labs. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: This is the only corporate item in the edition that Kenanga comments on itself, and the comment is deliberately cool. Kenanga acknowledges the strategic logic of powering YTLPOWER's data centre assets via captive generation but calls seven turbines totalling 5.25GW 'aggressive at this stage', takes a NEUTRAL stance on this specific development pending further clarity, and retains its OUTPERFORM rating and SoP-derived TP of RM6.40. A rating maintained alongside a neutral view on the news itself is the distinction to read: the call did not move because the development did not change the valuation.

What is missing is listed explicitly by Kenanga, not inferred here: deployment timelines, regulatory approvals, site locations, off-taker agreements and funding structures all remain pending. A reservation agreement is also not an order in the contractual sense - the item calls them reservation agreements throughout, and no purchase value, deposit or cancellation term appears anywhere.

The valuation already carries a smaller version of this. Kenanga states its SoP incorporates RM0.16/share of equity value for a prospective 1,400MW IPP project, on a 6.8% WACC, a 21-year concession period, 80:20 debt-to-equity financing, capex of USD1.0m/MW and a 100% equity stake. The 5,250MW now reserved is about 3.75 times that 1,400MW, and applying the same USD1.0m/MW capex assumption across the full fleet would imply roughly USD5.25b of capital - both figures are arithmetic here on Kenanga's own stated assumptions, and neither is printed. Kenanga applies the assumption only to the 1,400MW project.

Seven units for over 5,250MW implies an average unit size of about 750MW, computed here. Kenanga's own framing puts this against the company's announcement last month of plans to scale data centre capacity up to 2GW - so the generation reserved is more than twice the data centre capacity it is nominally intended to serve, which is part of why the comment reads as it does. The item itself claims no such ratio.

The share price context runs the other way and must not be read as a reaction. YTLPOWR fell 3.0% to RM5.51 on the 15 September session this edition reports, the third-largest decline among KLCI components behind PMETAL and YTL at -3.1% each; that session closed before this announcement, and Bursa was shut on 16 September for Malaysia Day. At RM5.51 the RM6.40 target implies about 16% upside - arithmetic here. This board last carried a YTLPOWR valuation on 3 September, in the Market Strategy row that recorded the same RM6.40 target raised on a pipeline of more than 1.1GW; the target is unchanged between the two.

news.h: PTT Synergy unit bags RM83.3m contract from Sime Darby Property
news.body: PTT Synergy Group Bhd's unit, Pembinaan Tetap Teguh Sdn Bhd (PTTSB), has secured a contract worth RM83.3m from Sime Darby Property Sdn Bhd. The contract involves performing earthworks and related tasks for multiple packages in Phase 1 of Bandar Bukit Raja Stage 4, located in Klang, Selangor. The group stated that the date of pre-possession shall be Sept 15, 2026; the date for possession shall commence on Sept 29, 2026; and the date for completion shall be Sept 28, 2027 and March 28, 2028 for Package 6 (Advance Unit for i34) and overall, respectively. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the largest of the edition's five corporate items and the only one with a full date schedule. Pre-possession 15 September 2026, possession from 29 September 2026, completion 28 September 2027 for Package 6 (Advance Unit for i34) and 28 March 2028 overall. Possession to overall completion is 18 months, which on RM83.3m implies an average of about RM4.6m of work a month - both the duration and the run-rate are arithmetic here, and neither is printed.

The scope is earthworks and related tasks for multiple packages in Phase 1 of Bandar Bukit Raja Stage 4 in Klang, Selangor. Earthworks sit at the front of a development programme, so this is an early-cycle award on a project whose later packages are not part of it; the item names no gross development value for the phase and no margin on the contract.

The counterparty is named as Sime Darby Property Sdn Bhd - a private entity as printed, not the Bursa-listed SIMEPROP, and the item draws no link between them. This board's most recent Kenanga figures on the listed company are the 26 August Results Note and the 3 September Market Strategy row, which recorded SIMEPROP as one of Kenanga's top picks at OUTPERFORM with a RM2.10 target. No report in the 17 September bundle covers property or construction.

This is PTT Synergy's third appearance on this board in under three weeks, and the first of the three that is an operating win. On 1 September it posted a higher 4Q net profit on a valuation gain with revenue down 27%, and on 14 September it bought Penang land for RM62.5m. A RM83.3m contract against a quarter in which revenue fell 27% is the most material of the three, but the item gives no revenue base to size it against and this board holds no Kenanga coverage of the company.

Nothing is disclosed about the economics. No margin, no payment schedule, no retention, no performance bond and no variation mechanism appears, and the item does not state PTT Synergy's ownership percentage in Pembinaan Tetap Teguh Sdn Bhd beyond calling it 'PTT Synergy Group Bhd's unit', so the share of RM83.3m accruing to the group cannot be established from the retrieved source.

news.h: UUE Holdings forms JV with Singapore-listed EGP Energy unit to tap power projects
news.body: UUE Holdings Bhd is forming a joint venture with a unit of Singapore-listed EGP Energy Corporation Ltd to build, develop and deliver power-grid infrastructure, including extra-high-voltage (EHV) electrical systems. UUE said the partnership marks a strategic expansion of its underground utilities engineering business into EHV substation engineering. Under the agreement, UUE's wholly-owned subsidiary Kum Fatt Engineering Sdn Bhd (KFE) will partner EGP Infrastructure Investments Pte Ltd (EGPII) to establish a Malaysian JV company - EGP-UUE Power System Engineering Sdn Bhd. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: Nothing is sized. No contract value, no capital commitment, no equity split between KFE and EGPII, no order book, no commencement date and no project is named. Of the edition's five corporate items this is the only one carrying no ringgit figure at all, which puts it in the same category as the 15 September DSR Taiko memorandum rather than with the three awards beside it.

The parties are precisely identified even though the economics are not: UUE's wholly-owned subsidiary Kum Fatt Engineering Sdn Bhd partners EGP Infrastructure Investments Pte Ltd, a unit of Singapore-listed EGP Energy Corporation Ltd, to establish a Malaysian JV company named EGP-UUE Power System Engineering Sdn Bhd. That KFE is wholly owned is stated; the JV's own shareholding is not.

The strategic content is a move up the voltage ladder. UUE describes it as a strategic expansion of its underground utilities engineering business into extra-high-voltage substation engineering - a different discipline from trenching and cable laying, and one where the partner rather than UUE appears to bring the capability. The item does not say what EGPII contributes, nor whether the JV has any pre-identified pipeline.

Grid infrastructure has been the most consistently recurring corporate theme on this board. PMW International secured an additional RM19.3m TNB contract on 27 August, MN Holdings' JV won RM67.3m of TNB cable works in Penang on 8 September, and HE Group took RM25.0m of power distribution works for a NAND flash manufacturer on 11 September - with MN Holdings' FY26 profits reported on 27 August as near-doubling on the data centre power infrastructure boom. This item extends that run into transmission-level work, and is the first of them with a foreign partner.

The structure is cross-border in one direction only: the capital partner is Singapore-listed, but the vehicle is Malaysian and the stated target is power-grid infrastructure without a named market. No report in the 17 September bundle covers UUE, utilities or engineering services - the bundle is two macro publications and carries no company report at all.

news.h: Ni Hsin unit to supply RM2.8m EVs to Alam Flora
news.body: Ni Hsin Group Bhd's wholly-owned subsidiary, Ni Hsin EV Tech Sdn Bhd (NHEVT), has secured two major purchase orders from waste management firm Alam Flora Sdn Bhd, a subsidiary of Malakoff Corp Bhd, for the supply of a fleet of electric vehicles for RM2.8m. It said in a statement the landmark cooperation highlights both companies' commitment to accelerating green initiatives and lowering carbon emissions within urban waste management and public sanitation sectors in Malaysia. The purchase includes 105 EV motorcycles valued at RM1.6m and 56 EV tricycles valued at RM1.2m. (The Star)
takeaways: The components reconcile exactly: 105 EV motorcycles at RM1.6m plus 56 EV tricycles at RM1.2m equals the RM2.8m headline. That implies about RM15,200 per motorcycle and about RM21,400 per tricycle - arithmetic here on the item's own figures, and the only unit economics it permits, since no margin, delivery schedule or servicing arrangement is given.

The scale and the language do not match, and both are carried as printed. The item calls these 'two major purchase orders' and a 'landmark cooperation' while the total is RM2.8m - roughly a thirtieth of the PTT Synergy award in the same edition and the smallest corporate figure this board has carried since the 27 August CC International tax client base acquisition at RM1.6m.

The buyer chain is the interesting part. Alam Flora Sdn Bhd is identified as a subsidiary of Malakoff Corp Bhd, so the end user sits inside a listed utility group, and the stated application is urban waste management and public sanitation. Neither Ni Hsin nor Malakoff is covered in the 17 September bundle, and this board holds no Kenanga rating on either.

It is one of two electric-vehicle items in this single edition, the other being NCER exploring EV and automotive investments as part of an RM470 billion target. One is a state-level ambition with no project attached and the other is a project with a small figure attached; between them they bracket where Malaysia's EV activity currently sits, though the digest places them in different sections and draws no link.

Provenance is worth noting: this is the only one of the five corporate items sourced to The Star rather than The Edge Malaysia. Two purchase orders are described but not separately valued beyond the motorcycle/tricycle split, and no repeat-order option, framework agreement or follow-on volume is mentioned, so nothing here can be annualised.

news.h: Crest Builder unit wins RM56.9m M&E subcontract from Pesona Metro
news.body: Crest Builder Holdings Bhd said its unit has won a mechanical and electrical (M&E) subcontract worth RM56.9m from a unit of construction company Pesona Metro Holdings Bhd. Crest Builder said a letter of award was given to its engineering unit CBTech (M) Sdn Bhd from Pesona Metro Sdn Bhd, which is the main contractor for the project. Under the subcontract, CBTech will supply, deliver, install, test, commission and maintain electrical services for the retail mall and Office Tower 1 components of the Ativo Annexe development in Bandar Sri Damansara, Selangor. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The scope runs past construction into operations. CBTech will supply, deliver, install, test, commission and maintain electrical services - the maintenance limb means part of the RM56.9m is recurring service work rather than build work, but the item gives no split between the two, no maintenance period and no completion date, so the revenue profile cannot be shaped from the retrieved source.

It is a subcontract, so the counterparty is a main contractor rather than a developer: Pesona Metro Sdn Bhd, a unit of listed Pesona Metro Holdings Bhd, is named as main contractor for the project. The end client and the development owner of the Ativo Annexe scheme in Bandar Sri Damansara, Selangor are not named, and no gross development value is given.

The work is confined to two named components - the retail mall and Office Tower 1 - which implies the wider development has further components not covered by this award. The item does not say whether CBTech is in line for them, and no framework or option is mentioned.

This is the third main-contractor subcontract this board has carried in three sessions, after Citaglobal's RM82.1m residential college subcontract on 14 September and Exsim Hospitality's RM42.5m building works subcontract on 15 September. All three are M&E or building services work sitting one layer below a named main contractor, and at RM56.9m this one sits between the other two in size - a pattern across editions rather than anything the digest observes.

Nothing about the economics or the ownership is disclosed. No margin, no payment terms and no stated ownership percentage in CBTech (M) Sdn Bhd beyond 'its engineering unit', so the share of RM56.9m accruing to Crest Builder cannot be established. No report in the 17 September bundle covers Crest Builder, Pesona Metro or construction.

macro.h: EU floats Canada becoming bloc's first 'associate member'
macro.body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union. She offered the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is a proposal from one office, not a decision by the bloc. The European Commission President made the offer in a state of the union address; no Council conclusion, member-state position, treaty mechanism or ratification step appears, and the item records no Canadian response even though Prime Minister Mark Carney was in the room.

'Associate member' is the whole of the item and it is left undefined. The status has no stated content - no customs arrangement, no single-market access, no budget contribution, no timetable - so there is nothing here a later edition can measure progress against.

The setting is doing some of the work: Strasbourg, a state of the union address, and the Canadian Prime Minister in attendance. That is a deliberate stage rather than a working-level negotiation, which is consistent with an invitation being floated rather than a text being tabled.

It continues a thread this board has been carrying for over a week. On 9 September the EU and Canada were reported planning a far-reaching alliance to strengthen partnership; this is the same trajectory arriving at a named status. It sits against the other half of Canada's year, which this board has recorded almost entirely through friction with the United States - retaliation after failed talks on 24 August, plans to hit Trump tariffs on 8 September, Carney framing retaliation as protective on 9 September, Trump predicting a deal 'fairly soon' on 14 September, and inflation holding at 3% on 15 September.

'Wednesday' is 16 September, the day before this edition and a day Bursa was closed for Malaysia Day - which is why this edition's market tables report the 15 September session. No market reaction to this item is therefore visible anywhere in the edition; the dating is read here from the calendar, not stated in the item.

macro.h: China and US discuss cutting tariffs on agriculture and energy - Bloomberg
macro.body: The US and China are discussing slashing tariffs on certain goods, including on American energy and agricultural shipments - a potential sign the leaders' summit next week will lead to an extension of the one-year trade truce. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: This is the first de-escalation item in a long run of the opposite. Since late August this board has carried the US eyeing China overcapacity tariffs of 7.5% before a Xi visit (27 August), the EU targeting China with 'Made in Europe' public-contract rules (10 September) and Germany preparing to lobby the EU for new China tariffs including on hybrid EVs (15 September). Today's item runs the other way, and the digest does not connect it to any of them.

Nothing is agreed and nothing is quantified. The parties are 'discussing slashing tariffs on certain goods'; no tariff rate, no product line beyond the two named categories, no negotiating round and no date for the leaders' summit beyond 'next week' appears.

The two named categories are both commodity exports - American energy and agricultural shipments. That is where a quick, politically legible cut is easiest, and it is notably not where the board's earlier items concentrated, which was manufactured goods, public procurement and technology.

A one-year trade truce is referred to as already in place, and the item's framing is that the summit may extend it. Neither the truce's start date nor its expiry is given, so how much time is actually at stake cannot be established from the retrieved source.

Provenance is second-hand and unattributed: the reporting is credited to Bloomberg via The Edge Malaysia, and no official on either side is quoted. It is one of three trade-architecture items among this edition's ten macro bits, alongside the EU's associate-membership offer to Canada and the WTO's reform warning - which makes trade the dominant macro theme of the edition, ahead of monetary policy for the first time in several sessions.

macro.h: WTO says global trade system at critical juncture, urges reform
macro.body: The World Trade Organization on Tuesday urged its members to reform global trade rules or risk a slide into fragmentation that could significantly reduce economic output and hit poorer countries hardest. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The warning is directional, not quantified. Fragmentation 'could significantly reduce economic output' - no estimate, no scenario, no time horizon and no baseline is given, so 'significantly' cannot be sized from the retrieved source.

No reform is actually proposed. The WTO 'urged its members to reform global trade rules'; the item names no rule, no negotiating agenda, no dispute-settlement fix and no member response, which leaves the item as a statement of urgency without a subject.

The distributional claim is the most specific thing in it: poorer countries would be hit hardest. That is the only distributional statement among this edition's ten macro bits, and the item offers no mechanism for why the incidence falls that way.

The same institution said something close to the opposite a week ago. On 10 September this board carried 'Global goods trade strengthening despite tariffs, Middle East tensions, WTO says'. Resilience then, a critical juncture now, from the same body within six sessions. They are not strictly contradictory - one describes current flows, the other the rules governing them - but the digest reconciles them nowhere, and the distinction is drawn here rather than in either item.

'Tuesday' is 15 September, the session this edition's market tables report, on which every one of the twelve indices in the table fell. No report in the 17 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on the WTO or on trade rules; the day's two publications are on the Federal Reserve and on domestic tactical positioning.

macro.h: Anwar: Govt to hold special meeting on Thursday to address rising electricity bills
macro.body: The government will hold a special meeting on Thursday to explore immediate mitigation measures following public outcry over surging electricity bills amid the recent hot weather and haze, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said on Wednesday. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The meeting is today. The Prime Minister spoke on Wednesday, 16 September, about a special meeting on Thursday - and this edition is dated Thursday, 17 September. The reader of this row is therefore ahead of the outcome, not behind it. That dating is read here from the two dates; the item does not state it.

The stated cause is weather, not policy: surging bills 'amid the recent hot weather and haze', which points at consumption volumes rather than at tariffs. No tariff change, no fuel-cost pass-through adjustment, no subsidy and no billing-cycle issue is named as the driver.

What is promised is exploration of 'immediate mitigation measures' - no measure, no cost, no allocation, no eligibility and no decision date. The word 'immediate' is the only indication of timing anywhere in the item.

TENAGA fell 2.4% to RM13.32 on the 15 September session reported in this edition, the fifth-largest decline among KLCI components, and PETGAS fell 1.1% to RM17.20. Those moves closed before Wednesday's statement and Bursa was shut on 16 September for Malaysia Day, so they are not a reaction to it. The digest draws no link and none should be read.

It is the first item specifically on electricity bills this board has carried, though energy costs have run through the Malaysian macro bits continuously: unsubsidised fuel prices up five sen on 27 August and down five sen on 3 September, six immediate cost-of-living measures and the Budi95 quota restoration on 1 September, and energy reform described as central to economic policy on 10 September. No report in the 17 September bundle covers TENAGA or the utilities sector - the only utilities content in the edition is Kenanga's own comment on YTL Power's turbine reservations.

macro.h: Malaysia, Japan agree to renew swap, promote local currencies settlements
macro.body: Malaysia and Japan have signed another bilateral swap agreement and agreed to a cooperation to promote the settlement of trade and investment in local currencies. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: Two distinct things are agreed and neither is sized. A bilateral swap agreement has been signed, and separately a cooperation to promote local-currency settlement of trade and investment. No facility size, no tenure, no signing date, no venue and no signatory institutions appear - the item does not even name the two central banks.

'Another' swap agreement indicates a renewal rather than a first. Because neither the previous size nor the new one is given, whether the facility was increased, held or reduced cannot be established from the retrieved source.

Local-currency settlement is the more structural of the two limbs: it is aimed at reducing dollar intermediation in bilateral flows. The item gives no mechanism, no target share, no participating banks and no timeline, so it is an intention rather than a measurable programme.

The scale it would apply to comes from an earlier edition, not this item: on 2 September this board recorded Malaysia-Japan trade up 11.8% to USD23.3b in January-July 2026. That is the denominator for any settlement-currency shift, and it is stated here rather than in the item.

The currency backdrop in this edition's own table cuts both ways. USD/MYR rose 0.26% to 4.0857 from 4.0753 and USD/YEN rose 0.18% to 154.85 from 154.57 - both currencies weakened against the dollar on the session, which is the condition that makes a local-currency settlement push attractive to both sides. The digest does not join them. The day's Economic Viewpoint separately expects the ringgit to weaken first after the Fed's hike before recovering toward 4.00, with the year-end forecast kept at 3.95.

macro.h: NCER explores EV, automotive investments as part of RM470.b target
macro.body: The Northern Corridor Economic Region (NCER) is exploring opportunities in the electric vehicle (EV) and automotive sectors as part of efforts to diversify investments beyond its strong electrical and electronics (E&E) and semiconductor base. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The RM470 billion is a target, not money committed. The item gives no deadline for it, no amount realised to date, no split by sector and no share attributable to the EV and automotive push it is reporting - so the headline figure and the subject of the item are not connected by anything measurable. The digest prints the figure as 'RM470.b' and it is carried here as printed, read as RM470 billion.
The activity described is exploration. NCER 'is exploring opportunities' in EV and automotive; no company, project, site, incentive or investment figure attaches to that leg anywhere in the item.

The motive stated is diversification, which is also an admission of concentration - NCER's base is described as strong in electrical and electronics and semiconductors, and the stated aim is to go beyond it. Those are precisely the sectors this board's recent content has clustered around: KGB's RM1.83b semiconductor wafer-fab award on 15 September, and Anwar and Modi discussing semiconductor cooperation on 14 September.

It is the second EV item in this single edition, alongside Ni Hsin's RM2.8m supply of 105 EV motorcycles and 56 EV tricycles to Alam Flora. One is a regional ambition with no project; the other is a project with a small figure. The EV theme has otherwise surfaced on this board only once, in the 26 August Budget 2027 proposals covering EV infrastructure and the Home Ownership Campaign.

It is a regional development corridor speaking, not a ministry, so no federal allocation or policy instrument follows from the retrieved source. No report in the 17 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on autos, EVs or the northern corridor.

macro.h: Southeast Asia growth divergence seen widening over next decade
macro.body: Southeast Asia's six largest economies are projected to grow on average 4.8% annually over the next decade, but widening structural differences put them on increasingly divergent paths. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: One figure, and it is an average over a decade: 4.8% annual growth for Southeast Asia's six largest economies. The item names no forecaster, no institution, no base year, no country-level path and not even which six economies are counted, so the number cannot be attributed or decomposed from the retrieved source.

The substance of the item is dispersion rather than the mean - widening structural differences putting the economies on increasingly divergent paths. None of those structural differences is identified, which leaves the claim unfalsifiable as printed.

The horizon is far longer than anything else on this board. Every other macro bit in this edition concerns a decision, a discussion, a statement or a monthly print; a ten-year regional average belongs in a different category and should be read as framing, not as a forecast a later edition can track.

Against Malaysia's own numbers as carried here, 4.8% sits below the house view for the current year: Kenanga's 2026 GDP growth forecast of 5.3% (2025: 5.2%) appears on this board in the 1 September Manufacturing PMI row and both 14 September Economic Viewpoint rows. The two are not comparable - one is a single-year national forecast, the other a ten-year six-country mean - and that comparison is drawn here, not in the item.

It is the only Asia Pacific bit in this edition, which is itself the break from pattern. Since 1 September the Bank of Japan has appeared in this board's Asia Pacific slot in at least six editions - a possible hike on 1 September, Takata on 3 September, a quarter-point preference on 4 September, 1997-high wage growth on 9 September, rapid-hike price risks on 11 September and non-linear inflation spikes on 15 September. There is no BOJ, no China data and no Japan monetary item today.

macro.h: Iran war has cost US military USD38.0b - Congressional Budget Office
macro.body: The war with Iran cost the US military around USD38 billion (RM153.7 billion) as of Aug 1, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday, with billions more potentially added to the price tag each month the conflict wears on. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the hardest-sourced number in the edition - around USD38 billion as of 1 August, from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office, stated Tuesday - and it is already six weeks stale at publication, with the CBO adding that billions more could accrue each month the conflict continues. No cumulative total, no end date and no monthly run-rate is given.

The ringgit conversion does not use the edition's own exchange rate. USD38 billion shown as RM153.7 billion implies about RM4.045 to the dollar, against the USD/MYR fix of 4.0857 printed in the same digest's forex table for the same day. The implied rate is arithmetic here; the discrepancy is small and is recorded rather than resolved.

What is measured is narrow: cost to the US military. No appropriation, no supplemental funding request, no share of the defence budget and no wider economic cost appears, so this is not a fiscal-impact figure and should not be read as one.

This conflict is the single largest driver of the numbers elsewhere in this edition. Nymex crude rose 4.38% to USD105.8 a barrel on the session reported - the largest move in the commodity table by a wide margin - and both of the day's Kenanga publications are built on it: the Economic Viewpoint describes the inflation impulse as an energy and geopolitical shock with Brent above USD100 and the Saudi East-West pipeline offline, while the Market Strategy cites disruption at Bab al-Mandeb and an EIA view that Middle East export hurdles persist through the end of 2026.

This board has carried the conflict continuously but never with a price attached until now: Qatari mediation as the US ramped up 'economic war' on 28 August, Iran using the Xi-Putin bloc to counter that on 2 September, renewed strike fears on 3 September, an ECB hike as the war fanned inflation fears on 11 September and Kazaks arguing for more on 15 September. This is the first item to put a dollar figure on it.

macro.h: US retail sales rebound sharply in August
macro.body: US retail sales rebounded more than expected in August as households stepped up purchases of motor vehicles and stocked up for the new school year, reinforcing the economy's resilience even as consumers grow more anxious about high inflation. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the only hard data release among this edition's ten macro bits, and it beat - retail sales rebounded more than expected in August. No percentage, no consensus figure and no prior-month reading is printed, so the size of the rebound or the surprise cannot be established from the retrieved source.

The composition is narrow and seasonal: motor vehicles and back-to-school stocking are the two drivers named. Neither is a durable signal about underlying consumption, and the item gives no control-group or ex-autos measure to strip them out.

The item carries its own contradiction and states it plainly - spending reinforcing the economy's resilience 'even as consumers grow more anxious about high inflation'. Behaviour and sentiment are pointing in opposite directions, which is exactly the configuration that makes the current policy argument hard to settle.

It lines up with the Fed's own revision as reported in the day's Economic Viewpoint, where the FOMC statement describes domestic spending as 'resilient', productivity as 'strong' and capital investment as 'robust', and the projections lift 2026 growth to 2.3% and cut unemployment to 4.1%. This print is the kind of evidence behind that language, published the morning after the decision.

US activity data has surprised upward in every print this board has carried for three weeks - service-sector-led acceleration on 24 August, strong services demand on 4 September, and a surge in August non-farm payrolls with unemployment steady at 4.1% on 7 September - alongside the 11 September producer-price print and the 14 September consumer inflation pick-up. Kenanga's own note says the August CPI print settled the hike; consumption this strong on top of it removes the last data argument for the hold it had forecast.

macro.h: French central bank trims growth outlook
macro.body: France faces sluggish growth this year as consumers rein in spending and businesses hold back investment over uncertainty about energy prices, public finances and geopolitical tensions, the central bank said on Tuesday, trimming its outlook. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: A downgrade with no number attached. The central bank trimmed its outlook on Tuesday, but neither the previous forecast nor the revised one is printed, so the size of the cut cannot be established from the retrieved source and no later edition can measure a further revision against it.

All three causes named sit on the demand and confidence side: consumers reining in spending, businesses holding back investment, and uncertainty over energy prices, public finances and geopolitical tensions. Notably absent is any reference to interest rates, even though the ECB raised them on 11 September.

Energy prices appear here as a growth cost, which is the half of the shock the board's European items have mostly not carried. The same oil move that this edition prints as Nymex crude up 4.38% to USD105.8 - and that the day's Economic Viewpoint calls a supply shock the Fed cannot fix with rates - shows up in France as suppressed household and business spending.

It is the first counterweight in an otherwise one-directional European run. This board has carried the ECB raising rates as the Iran war fanned inflation fears on 11 September, Lagarde calling the inflation shock longer-lasting on 14 September, and Kazaks seeing a growing case for more tightening on 15 September. A national central bank inside the same currency union trimming growth is the other side of that trade-off, and the digest does not set the two against each other.

Public finances being named as a source of uncertainty is the one country-specific element, and the item develops it no further - no deficit figure, no budget process and no rating action appears. FTSE-100 fell 0.37% to 10,658.1 on the session reported, one of twelve index declines in a table containing no gains at all, and no report in the 17 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on France or the euro area.

reports.flag: Six points of caution on this row, reported as printed rather than resolved. (1) One target price disagrees with this board's own earlier row. The note prints CIMB as (OP; TP: RM8.30); this board's 1 September Results Note on CIMB, read from CIMB's own report PDF, carries OUTPERFORM with a target of RM8.35. The five-sen gap cannot be resolved from the retrieved sources and neither figure is used as this row's data - the row carries no rating or target of its own. (2) The MGS baseline is given two ways on the same page. Page 2 states that 10-year MGS yields 'had spiked from 3.7% to the current more than 4.1%' on BNM information, while the sensitivity analysis in the same section assumes yields 'rising to c4.1%, versus 3.6% as at end of 2Q26'. A 3.7% or a 3.6% starting point changes the size of the revaluation being estimated. (3) The KLFIN decline is given two ways. Page 1: the index 'has slipped more than 2% since end-August'. Page 2: 'almost 3% KLFIN dip since August'. Both are reproduced. (4) The stated devaluation and the stated ringgit amount do not quite agree. A 'c2% devaluation' applied to a RM126b FVTPL book is described as amounting to RM2.3b; RM2.3b on RM126b is 1.83%. The gap is within the note's own 'roughly estimate' framing but is identified here, not in the document. (5) Two exhibit cross-references point at the wrong exhibits. The text directs the reader to 'exhibit 1' for the December 2026, June 2027 and December 2027 futures contracts - that chart is Exhibit 10, while Exhibit 1 is the banks' fixed-income securities table - and to 'exhibit 4' for the technology sector's negative correlation with oil, which is Exhibit 12, while Exhibit 4 is the fixed-deposit maturity mix. (6) The note quotes ratings and target prices for stocks that have no standalone report in this day's bundle - MAYBANK, HLBANK, ABMB, CIMB, MISC, PCHEM, WPRTS, SUNREIT, PAVREIT and KPJ. Those figures are as quoted in this strategy piece and have not been independently verified against stock-specific reports today; where this board holds an earlier Kenanga row for the same stock the two agree, except for CIMB as set out in point (1).

reports.name: Rate Reactions: Tactical Responses to Higher Oil and Bond Yield Environment
reports.catalyst: A positioning note written in the hours after the Fed's 25bps hike, not a ratings or index-target revision - no call and no target price is changed in it. Four tactical conclusions: within banks stay with MAYBANK, HLBANK and ABMB rather than AMBANK and CIMB while bond-yield revaluation runs through 3Q26 results; look at defensives and REITs on valuation, with SUNREIT and PAVREIT preferred and the recent KPJ upgrade cited, though the REIT yield spread over MGS is explicitly 'not yet' at a level consistent with a bullish sector call; own oil and gas through MISC rather than high-beta PCHEM because the futures curve shows the spike concentrated in near-dated contracts; and consider trimming WPRTS as a negatively correlated offset. Kenanga's view is for the OPR to hold and for the 10-year MGS yield to taper to 3.88%.
reports.quote: The combination of high bond yields and oil causes us to explore several tactical positioning.
summary: Read what this note is before reading what it says. It changes no rating, no target price and no index target; it is a tactical overlay on positions Kenanga already holds, written around a rate decision that had just landed - the text opens with 'at time of writing the US Federal Reserve has proceeded with a rate hike of 25 bps'. Its framing argument is that rate hikes do not solve supply-driven inflation, with oil above USD100 a barrel on the US-Iran conflict, so the combination of high bond yields and high oil is what the portfolio has to be positioned against. The same bundle's Economic Viewpoint makes the identical argument about the Fed in stronger terms, and the two notes agree on the two numbers they share: a 10-year MGS yield tapering to 3.88% and the OPR held at 2.75%.

The bank case is a revaluation-timing argument, and its arithmetic mostly reconciles. Across the eight anchor banking groups Kenanga puts about RM530b of assets in revaluation-sensitive fixed income - FVTPL and FVOCI, excluding amortised cost - or about 15% of the asset base, which implies a combined asset base of roughly RM3.5 trillion, computed here. Those holdings rose about 5% QoQ or RM24b in 2Q26. Assuming the 10-year MGS at c4.1% against the 2Q26 level, Kenanga estimates a c2% devaluation on an average four-year tenure; applied to the RM126b FVTPL book that is RM2.3b, or 6% of the eight banks' aggregate net profit - which implies aggregate net profit near RM38b, also computed here. The impact halves to about 3% as yields taper. Two figures in that chain do not line up cleanly and are recorded in this row's flag: the starting yield is given as both 3.7% and 3.6%, and RM2.3b on RM126b is 1.83% rather than 2%.

The 'largely priced in' claim rests on two observations worth separating. Kenanga argues the KLFIN index has already absorbed the c3% earnings risk, having fallen since end-August - stated as 'more than 2%' on page 1 and 'almost 3%' on page 2, both carried. Separately it puts the equity risk premium over MGS at 2.8% against a ten-year average of about 3%, reading the shortfall as part of recent market weakness, and notes the KLCI is down close to 3% in September. It also states the MGS move is not a foreign-selling story: foreigners remained net buyers in August and month-to-date in September, with ASEAN yields rising alongside US Treasuries. Against that, this edition's own participation table shows foreign investors as net sellers of RM17.5m on the 15 September session - a single session against a month-to-date claim, so not a contradiction, but not the same measure either, and the comparison is drawn here rather than in the note.

On REITs, Kenanga states the exact condition that would change its call and then declines to meet it. The sector has slumped 7% year-to-date; historically a REIT yield of around 2.5% above MGS has been consistent with a more bullish sector index rise; the spread is currently 2.0%. So the note says the sector is closing in on that level but is explicitly 'not yet' there, and stays selective with SUNREIT (OP; TP: RM2.45) and PAVREIT (OP; TP: RM1.95). On traditionally defensive sectors it points to its recent upgrade of KPJ (OP; TP: RM3.05) as evidence of being slightly more constructive on hospitals - while keeping the sector at NEUTRAL - and attributes the upgrade to valuation after share-price slippage following a management departure. This board carried that KPJ Company Update on 9 September at the same OUTPERFORM and the same RM3.05 target, so the two rows agree.

The oil recommendation is deliberately unexciting, and the day's prices sharpen why. Kenanga cites the US EIA expecting Middle East export hurdles to persist through the end of 2026, keeping regional production below pre-conflict averages until 2Q27, and argues oil exposure hedges the Treasury-yield risk carried by technology holdings. But the futures curve shows the spike concentrated in near-dated contracts, with June 2027 and December 2027 more benign, so it resists chasing PCHEM (MP; TP: RM4.24) as it did in the earlier episode and prefers MISC (OP; TP: RM9.20) as a more enduring play on elevated 2027 prices and high tonne-mile demand from route disruption; it also floats trimming WPRTS (MP; TP: RM6.20) as a negatively correlated offset. Two price observations, computed here from the same morning's digest and absent from the note: MISC closed at RM7.95 on 15 September as the top gainer among KLCI components at +1.8%, about 16% below its RM9.20 target, while PCHEM closed at RM5.20 - roughly 23% ABOVE its own RM4.24 target, a Market Perform trading well through Kenanga's valuation. On conviction: this row reads Positive because the note names its picks in Kenanga's own words, calling MAYBANK, HLBANK and ABMB 'our top picks'. The other two phrases found by this board's full search - 'our preference for SUNREIT and PAVREIT' and 'we like MISC' - are recorded as investment-case language rather than pick declarations, the same treatment this board gave 'We like KGB for' on 15 September and 'We like BAUTO for' on 11 September.

On the REIT preference, the coverage is dense and recent. The Star, 14 August 2026, carries four named houses on SUNREIT after its results: TA Research upgraded to Buy from Hold with a RM2.79 target on a 2027 target yield of 5% plus a 3% ESG premium; CIMB Research upgraded to Buy from Hold with a RM2.55 target, citing 'sequentially stronger earnings in 2H26, supported by more public holidays and improving hotel bookings'; Hong Leong Investment Bank kept Buy at RM2.48 on a 5.3% target yield; and MBSB Research kept Buy at RM2.39. The same article records Kenanga at Outperform with a RM2.45 target - the identical rating and target this 17 September note repeats a month later. All four named houses point the same way as Kenanga, so the divergence marker is not set, and none of them used pick language. On the bank picks, the most recent retrievable house declaration is three months old and only partly overlaps. The Edge Malaysia reported on 24 June 2026 that CIMB Securities kept an Overweight on Malaysian banks entering a new valuation cycle, with top picks Hong Leong Bank (TP RM26.40), RHB Bank (TP RM9.20) and Public Bank (TP RM5.50), on the argument that the banks deserving premium valuations are those that consistently convert excess capital into dividends and special distributions. Read the dating carefully: that note predates this one by nearly three months and does not respond to the Fed hike or to the MGS move that drives Kenanga's tactical switch, so under this board's most-recent-statement rule it is the latest retrievable CIMB Securities sector call rather than a comparable view. The one name both houses put forward is HLBANK; Kenanga's tactical trio adds MAYBANK and ABMB and explicitly prefers them to AMBANK and CIMB, while CIMB Securities' own list contains neither of those two and instead carries RHB Bank and Public Bank. What could not be retrieved, stated precisely: a Business Today report dated 11 September 2026, headlined as RHB staying Neutral on banks amid funding pressure and asset-quality risks, returned HTTP 403 under every retrieval attempt made in this run, so its contents were not read and are not used here or cited. The note states 'We maintain our year-end USDMYR forecast of 3.95 but see 4.00 as the more realistic near-term anchor' - so the published forecast and the number the note actually expects are different, and the spot fix printed in the same morning's digest is 4.0857. reports.name: US FOMC Meeting (15-16 September): Unanimous hike into a supply shock; 2Q27 cut dropped for an extended hold
reports.catalyst: The Fed raised the target range by 25bps to 3.75%-4.00% in a unanimous 12-0 vote, its first increase in more than three years. Kenanga had forecast a hold and says so directly. It calls the hike a policy error on the grounds that the inflation impulse is an energy and geopolitical shock a higher funds rate cannot supply into, leans to one-and-done rather than a cycle, drops its 2Q27 first-cut call, and moves to a base case of an extended hold at 3.75%-4.00% through end-2027. Forecasts kept: year-end USDMYR 3.95 with 4.00 named the more realistic near-term anchor, end-2026 10-Y UST 4.80%, end-2026 10-Y MGS 3.88%, and the OPR at 2.75%.
reports.quote: We think the hike was a policy error.
summary: The decision, the vote, and an explicit admission. The Fed raised the target range 25bps to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase since 2023, on a 12-0 vote in which July's three hawkish dissenters were joined by the entire committee, Warsh included. Kenanga's own Table 3 records its house outlook for the 15-16 September meeting as 'No change' against a Fed Funds futures reading of a 25bps hike and an actual 25bps hike, and the text does not soften it: 'We expected a hold and were wrong on the meeting.' The note's stated reason the market got there first is that the move had been priced since Jackson Hole - which this board carried as an Economic Viewpoint on 1 September - and that the August CPI print settled it, an item carried here on 14 September.

The statement change Kenanga treats as the real news is a deletion rather than an addition. July attributed elevated inflation 'in part' to supply shocks in certain sectors including energy; September removes that clause and replaces it with 'today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal'. The activity language moved the opposite way - domestic spending 'resilient', productivity 'strong', capital investment 'robust'. Kenanga's reading is that the Fed has stopped describing the inflation problem as supply-driven, and that this was precisely the framing which justified patience two months ago. The 17 September digest's own macro bits carry the corroborating data point on the activity side: US retail sales rebounding more than expected in August.

The press conference removed accommodation and offered nothing about the path. Warsh framed the move narrowly - the committee 'removed a dose of accommodation' so that credit and financial conditions align with the mandate - and repeated that he would be hard-pressed to call conditions restrictive. He named three things that changed since July: stronger labour data, elevated summer inflation and geopolitics. He declined to discuss the neutral rate, declined the path ahead with 'I'm not in the forward guidance business', declined to discuss his conversations with the President, rejected the suggestion that markets drove the decision, and again withheld his own dot. Kenanga's summary of the message is discipline over direction - the Fed will act on the standard set at Jackson Hole and will not say when.

The dot plot says one more and then a long plateau, and the market does not believe it. The median participant sees the funds rate at 4.1% at end-2026, implying one further hike, holds it there through 2027, then eases to 3.9% in 2028 and 3.6% in 2029. Twelve of eighteen participants pencilled one more hike this year, four see two and two see none - which accounts for the full committee - and only four project any cut in 2027. The projections moved with the rate: growth revised up to 2.3% and 2.4% for 2026 and 2027, unemployment down to 4.1%, core PCE up to 3.4% for 2026, with inflation risks skewed to the upside and labour risks balanced. Markets price roughly three further hikes, well above the median, and that gap is the note's stated risk rather than an inference here.

What Kenanga actually changed, and what it kept. It calls the hike a policy error on a specific argument: the inflation impulse is an energy and geopolitical shock - Brent above USD100, the Saudi East-West pipeline offline - and a higher funds rate adds no supply while tightening credit and raising the cost of capital in an economy already absorbing an external price shock. Its risk case is that markets test the Fed again if oil stays elevated and headline inflation does not fall. It therefore leans to one-and-done rather than a cycle, attaches the next move to no month, and drops the 2Q27 first-cut call that had rested on Brent averaging USD80 in 2026; the base case becomes an extended hold at 3.75%-4.00% through end-2027. On markets it expects initial USD strength with the ringgit weakening first and recovering toward 4.00 as a December move fades from pricing, keeps the year-end USDMYR forecast at 3.95 while calling 4.00 the more realistic near-term anchor, and describes bear flattening in Treasuries with the 10-Y back above 5.00% against an end-2026 forecast of 4.80% it concedes now sits below spot. For Malaysia it reads the MGS sell-off as spillover from higher UST yields plus a rebuilt term premium ahead of Budget 2027, not a repricing of BNM, and maintains end-2026 10-Y MGS at 3.88% and the OPR at 2.75% - both identical to the figures in the Market Strategy note published in the same bundle. Searching the note for this board's full conviction list - top pick, sector pick, our pick, preferred, most attractive, we like, favour, favourite - returns nothing, and no stock is named anywhere in it, so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated and no Analyst Signal is sought.
